Data quality checks are used to identify incorrect, incomplete, inconsistent, or unexpected data before it affects downstream consumers.

Completeness checks verify that required fields are populated and that expected records are present.

Uniqueness checks detect duplicate values in columns that should contain unique identifiers.

Validity checks verify that values conform to expected formats, ranges, or allowed categories.

Referential integrity checks verify that foreign keys have corresponding records in related dimension or reference tables.

Freshness checks determine whether data arrived within the expected time window.

Row-count checks compare the number of records against expected thresholds or historical patterns.

Data quality failures should be observable and actionable. A pipeline can record failed checks, affected datasets, batch identifiers, and error details.

Quarantine mechanisms can isolate invalid records while allowing valid records to continue through the pipelin

e when the business process permits it.

Quality metrics can also be used for monitoring trends over time, helping teams identify gradual deterioration in source data.

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform used to publish, store, and consume streams of records.

Kafka organizes records into topics. Topics are divided into partitions, which provide parallelism and allow multiple consumers to process different partitions concurrently.

Producers publish records to Kafka topics. Consumers read records from topics and track their progress using offsets.

A consumer group allows multiple consumer instances to coordinate processing. Each partition is normally assigned to one consumer within a consumer group at a time.

Kafka retains records according to configured retention policies. Consumers can process records at their own pace within the available retention period.

Partitioning is important for Kafka scalability. Records with the same key are normally routed to the same partition, which can preserve ordering for that key.

Kafka is commonly used as an ingestion layer for streaming data pipelines. Downstream systems can consume events
and transform, enrich, validate, or store them.

A production data pipeline typically moves data through several stages including ingestion, validation, transformation, quality checks, and publishing.

The ingestion stage reads data from source systems and records metadata such as source name, ingestion timestamp, batch identifier, and schema information.

Validation checks whether the incoming data conforms to the expected schema and business rules. Invalid records can be quarantined instead of being allowed into downstream processing.

Transformation converts raw data into business-ready structures. Common operations include filtering, joining dimension tables, deduplication, normalization, aggregation, and deriving calculated fields.

A pipeline should maintain data quality checks at important processing boundaries. Examples include null checks, duplicate detection, referential integrity, row-count validation, and accepted-value checks.

Production pipelines should also provide observability. Useful operational metadata includes p

ipeline status, processing duration, input row count, output row count, error count, and execution identifier.

Incremental processing compares incoming data with previously processed data and processes only new or changed records. This can reduce unnecessary computation when source datasets are large.

A reliable pipeline should be idempotent where possible. Re-running the same batch should not create unintended duplicate records or inconsistent output.

Snowflake uses virtual warehouses to provide compute resources for executing SQL queries and data processing workloads.

A virtual warehouse is a cluster of compute resources that can execute queries independently from Snowflake storage.

Warehouse size controls the amount of compute available to a workload. Larger warehouses can provide more compute capacity but generally increase compute consumption.

Multi-cluster warehouses can add clusters when concurrency increases. This is useful when many queries need to execute at the same time.

Warehouse auto-suspend can stop an inactive warehouse after a configured period. Auto-resume can start it again when a new workload arrives.

For data engineering workloads, warehouse selection can be based on workload characteristics such as input data size, query complexity, concurrency, and execution requirements.

A dynamic warehouse allocation strategy can map workload sizes to different warehouse configurations. For example, a small input batch

can use a small warehouse while a large transformation workload can use a larger warehouse.

Query history and warehouse monitoring can be used to analyze execution time, resource consumption, and workload behavior.

Apache Spark is a distributed data processing engine designed to process large datasets across a cluster.

A Spark application consists of a driver process and executor processes. The driver coordinates the application, creates the execution plan, and schedules work. Executors run tasks assigned by the driver and store data for computation.

When an action is triggered, Spark creates a job. The job is divided into stages based on shuffle boundaries. Stages are further divided into tasks. A task is the smallest unit of work sent to an executor.

Spark uses partitions to divide a dataset into smaller pieces that can be processed in parallel. Each task normally operates on one partition. The scheduler assigns tasks to available executor cores.

Executors can run multiple tasks concurrently depending on the number of cores allocated to them. This parallel execution allows Spark to process large datasets across multiple machines.

Shuffle operations move data between executors. Operations s
uch as groupBy, join, and repartition can introduce shuffle boundaries and may require network and disk I/O.

Spark performance depends on partitioning, parallelism, serialization, memory usage, shuffle behavior, and the amount of data processed.

Partitioning determines how data is distributed across tasks. Too few partitions can reduce parallelism, while too many small partitions can increase scheduling overhead.

A shuffle occurs when Spark needs to redistribute data across executors. Large shuffles can become expensive because data may need to be serialized, transferred across the network, and written to disk.

Broadcast joins can improve performance when one side of a join is small enough to be distributed to executors. This can avoid a large shuffle of the smaller dataset.

Caching or persisting a DataFrame can help when the same computed dataset is reused multiple times. However, caching consumes executor memory and should be used selectively.

Spark executors have limited memory. Poor memory configuration, large objects, data skew, and excessive aggregation can lead to spills or out-of

-memory errors.

Data skew occurs when some partitions contain significantly more data than others. A skewed partition can create a straggler task while other executors finish early.

Performance tuning should be based on execution metrics rather than assumptions. Spark UI metrics can be used to inspect stages, task duration, shuffle read, shuffle write, input size, and executor behavior.
